changelog: Eight builds' worth of fixes since 0.0.49, most of them found on a phone. Nothing about how the game plays has changed — this is all about whether you can see and read what it is doing. On a phone, the board is usable again It fits the screen properly. Fitting the whole board by its binding axis is right on a desktop and wrong on a phone held sideways, where that axis is always the height: a 22x14 board came out at fifteen pixels a tile with 62% of the width sitting empty — a small rectangle marooned on a large wooden table. Tiles now grow until they are actually readable, capped so the board can never overflow sideways. You pan vertically, which is the axis a hand of cards already trains you to expect. Measured: 15px to 30px a tile, width fill 38% to 76%. Pinch is smooth again. Zooming tore horizontally and the frame meter sat red at 145 of 240 frames over budget. The board had quietly fallen off its own compositor layer — the camera rewrite began writing an inline transform that overrode the hint holding it there — so every gesture frame was re-drawing the entire wood surface and every tile on the main thread. On top of that the camera was re-measuring the page mid-gesture, and with tile culling on, one measurement means re-deciding which tiles are on screen. Both are fixed; a pinch is a compositor move again. Moving units are actually drawn A travelling piece was being erased for its whole journey. A unit belongs to the tile it moves to and spends its flight rendered back over the tile it came from, which puts it outside its own cell for almost the entire trip — and tile culling clips a cell's contents to exactly that box. So the unit sank behind the board and slid back into view at the destination. It had been broken since the culling landed, two weeks before the travel animation was written. Pieces also stopped painting behind the tiles in some frames, and the resting drop shadow no longer vanishes at each end of a hop. The board reads better The table is no longer painted underneath solid cloud. An unexplored tile is covered corner to corner, and the wood beneath it was being drawn anyway — on a mostly-unexplored map that is a lot of tiles rendering a texture with no pixels to show for it. Explored-but-remembered tiles are untouched: their terrain is meant to read through the veil. Tapping a tile tells you the truth The Legend promises you can tap anything to inspect it, and four things quietly broke that promise. The objective tile had no case at all — it described the ground it stands on, "Open Ground", while the HUD counted down against that very tile. The storm's eye — the one square the storm's own text tells you to shelter on — reported itself as bare ground. A node drew a blank square where its art should be, and claimed "+1 max CP" whichever kind it was, so a draw node advertised a reward it does not give. Nodes, workshops and voids had names but no description at all. The panels talk to a player now. The tag list is gone: `infantry · tribe` and `structure · tribe_camp` were the engine's own internal labels printed verbatim, underscores and all, and everything they hinted at is already said properly above them. Unit intent is words rather than a speck of an icon — and "hold" never had an icon in the first place, so it rendered as "Intent: · holding". Decorative symbols are out of the explanatory text generally, including one that pointed you at a diamond shape that the board almost never actually draws. Symbols that are the thing rather than punctuation inside a sentence — damage and kill markers, the keep star on a card, card category glyphs, map icons, the victory banner — are all untouched. What desktop players get The move-animation fix, the fog and table fix, every tile-inspection fix and all the copy work. The board-fit change is measured as byte-identical on desktop by design: it only raises a floor that desktop sizes were already well above. The compositor fix helps panning a large board there too.
